title: Moon First or Mars First?
resolution: Resolved: NASA should land astronauts on the Moon again before sending astronauts to Mars.
summary: NASA plans to return astronauts to the Moon's surface and use what it learns to prepare for Mars. Some argue the Moon is a needed proving ground; others say it's a costly detour from the bigger goal. Which should come first?

background.p: No one has walked on the Moon since Apollo 17 in December 1972. NASA's Artemis program aims to go back. On Artemis II, four astronauts (Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch of NASA and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency) flew around the Moon, launching April 1, 2026, and splashing down in the Pacific on April 10, 2026.

In February 2026, NASA changed its plan. Artemis III, set for 2027, became a test flight in low Earth orbit, where astronauts will practice docking with commercial Moon landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin and test new spacesuits. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is to be the first landing, and NASA said it aims for at least one landing a year after that. NASA restated this timeline in October 2026.

NASA's Moon to Mars objectives (September 2022) call for missions on and around the Moon "followed by missions to Mars," using the Moon partly to test systems for Mars. Mars is much harder: a NASA workshop paper describes an example round trip of about 850 days, a one-way radio delay of up to about 22 minutes, and notes that lessons from lunar mission aborts will have limited direct use for Mars, since an early return from Mars could take hundreds of days. The Moon program is expensive: NASA's Inspector General projected in 2021 that the agency would spend about $93 billion on the Artemis effort through fiscal year 2025.

disputed.q: How much does practice on the Moon help with Mars?
positions: NASA's plans hold that landing, living and working on the Moon tests the systems, suits and operations Mars will need, close enough to Earth to come home if something fails.
Critics say the Moon's lack of air, its weaker gravity and its short distance from Earth make it a poor stand-in, so Moon hardware and practice may not carry over well to Mars.

terms.def: NASA's program to return astronauts to the Moon, using the Space Launch System rocket, the Orion capsule and commercial landers.
Orbit a few hundred miles above Earth, where the International Space Station flies.
A place to test equipment and skills before using them where failure would be more dangerous.
A period when a launch can reach its target efficiently. Good windows to Mars come about every 26 months.

aff.label: Affirmative (Moon first)
aff.stance: The Moon is close, reachable and a safe place to learn the skills and test the machines a Mars mission will depend on.

args.claim: The Moon is a safer place to learn.
args.warrant: The Moon is about three days from Earth. If something goes wrong, a crew can come home in days. At Mars, help is months away, so mistakes must be found and fixed first.
args.evidence: NASA's Moon to Mars objectives, which call for using the Moon to shorten testing before Mars; NASA's Mars challenges paper on long abort times.
args.response: The negative answers that the Moon tests the wrong things: NASA's own paper says lessons from lunar aborts will have limited direct use at Mars.

args.claim: We need to test life support and suits on another world.
args.warrant: Astronauts will need to live for long periods away from Earth, wear suits in harsh dust and work outside daily. The Moon lets NASA test all of this on a real surface.
args.evidence: Artemis plans for surface stays and new spacesuits; NASA's architecture documents on Mars-forward tests at the Moon.
args.response: The negative replies that the space station and Earth-based tests can do much of this without the cost of landings.

args.warrant: Artemis II has flown, landers are being built and a 2028 landing is planned. Changing direction now would waste years of work and money and could leave the nation with neither goal.
args.evidence: NASA's 2026 Artemis updates; history of programs canceled midstream, such as Constellation in 2010.
args.response: The negative answers that money already spent is gone either way (the sunk cost fallacy), and the question is what's best from here.

args.claim: The Moon has science and resources of its own.
args.warrant: The Moon's craters hold clues to the early solar system, and ice near the south pole might one day supply water and fuel. These are worth exploring for their own sake.
args.evidence: NASA lunar science goals; studies of water ice at the lunar south pole.
args.response: The negative replies that robots can study the Moon cheaply, and that Mars may hold the bigger scientific prize: signs of past life.

neg.label: Negative (Mars first)
neg.stance: Mars is the goal that matters most, and spending decades and billions on the Moon delays it without preparing for it well.

args.warrant: Mars once had liquid water and may have had life. Astronauts there could search in ways robots can't, so the most important science is on Mars, not the Moon.
args.evidence: NASA Mars science goals; findings from Mars rovers about ancient water.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the science will still be there in a decade, and getting astronauts home safely matters more than getting there first.

args.claim: The Moon is a poor practice ground for Mars.
args.warrant: Mars has an atmosphere, stronger gravity, long communication delays and trips measured in years. Landing on the Moon teaches different skills, so Moon hardware may not carry over.
args.evidence: NASA's 2024 Mars challenges workshop paper, noting an 850-day example mission, 22-minute one-way delays and limited lessons from lunar aborts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that life support, suits, surface operations and long missions far from Earth all carry over, even if landing does not.

args.warrant: NASA's budget is a small, fairly flat share of federal spending. Every dollar and year spent on lunar landings is a dollar and year not spent on Mars.
args.evidence: NASA Inspector General (2021): about $93 billion on Artemis through fiscal year 2025 and about $4.1 billion for each launch of the rocket and capsule through Artemis IV; NASA's small, flat share of federal spending.
args.response: The affirmative answers that Mars systems, such as landers and life support, can be built while the Moon program runs, and Congress decides the budget.

args.claim: We've already been to the Moon.
args.warrant: Apollo landed twelve astronauts on the Moon. A bold new goal can inspire students and the public and draw support in a way a return trip may not.
args.evidence: Apollo history; surveys of public interest in space goals.
args.response: The affirmative replies that Apollo made short visits, and learning to stay and work on the Moon is a new and harder goal.

strawmen.strawman: They just want to redo Apollo because it's familiar.
strawmen.why: Supporters argue for long stays, new technology and safety testing close to home, which Apollo never did.
strawmen.steelman: The Moon is days from Earth, so it's the safest place to test the life support, suits and surface work Mars will require before risking a crew months from help.

strawmen.strawman: They want to rush astronauts to Mars no matter the danger.
strawmen.why: Mars-first supporters usually want careful testing too, but through other means than lunar landings.
strawmen.steelman: Mars holds the biggest scientific questions, and the Moon differs from Mars so much that landing there may delay Mars without preparing for it well.

weak.arg: We have to beat other countries to the Moon.
weak.why: Competition may matter, but it doesn't show that the Moon must come before Mars; tie your case to preparation and safety.
It's a feeling, not an argument, and it ignores the Moon's science and its use as a test site.
